lead: Restoration filters clean a noisy image when blur is absent: g(x,y) = f(x,y) + n(x,y), where g is the observed image, f is the true image and n is the noise. The filter must match the noise. Averaging suits Gaussian noise, order statistics delete impulses, and adaptive filters vary strength with local variance. Only a few universities teach this topic at this depth. Phone cameras, CCTV cleanup and medical scans use these cheap neighbourhood operations before any inverse or Wiener stage.
prereq: You need noise types from 3.2 and neighbourhood smoothing from Unit 2.

blocks.text: Let S_xy be an M×N window centred at (x,y), and g(s,t) a noisy pixel in it. The arithmetic mean is f̄ = (1/MN) Σ g(s,t). The geometric mean is [Π g(s,t)]^{1/MN}. The harmonic mean is MN / Σ [1/g(s,t)]. The contraharmonic mean is Σ g(s,t)^{Q+1} / Σ g(s,t)^Q, where Q is a real order. Q = 0 gives the arithmetic mean; Q > 0 removes pepper (dark spots); Q < 0 removes salt (bright spots). Averaging blurs edges. The harmonic mean handles salt noise but fails on pepper because a near-zero pixel makes 1/g large.

Order-statistic filters sort the MN values and pick a rank. The median is the middle value, at position (MN+1)/2 for odd MN. It deletes salt-and-pepper impulses because they sit at extreme ranks. The max filter outputs the largest value; it removes pepper noise. The min filter outputs the smallest value; it removes salt noise. The midpoint is (z_min + z_max)/2, where z_min and z_max are the smallest and largest values. It suits Gaussian or uniform noise but one impulse ruins it. The alpha-trimmed mean sorts the values, deletes d/2 from each end (d even), and averages the rest. d is the number trimmed, 0 ≤ d ≤ MN−1. d = 0 gives the arithmetic mean; d = MN−1 gives the median. A large median window can erase thin lines.

Adaptive filters read local statistics before smoothing. The adaptive local noise reduction filter is f̂(x,y) = g(x,y) − (σ²ₙ / σ²_L) [g(x,y) − m_L]. Here g is the noisy pixel, m_L is the local mean, σ²_L is the local variance, and σ²ₙ is the noise variance. In a flat region σ²_L ≈ σ²ₙ, so the ratio is near 1 and the output is close to m_L: strong smoothing. At an edge σ²_L ≫ σ²ₙ, so the ratio is near 0 and the output stays close to g: no smoothing.

The adaptive median filter grows a window from 3×3 up to S_max, the largest allowed window size. Let z_min, z_med, z_max be the smallest, median and largest values, and z_xy the centre pixel. If z_min < z_med < z_max, go to level B; otherwise enlarge the window. If the window reaches S_max, output z_med. At level B, output z_xy if z_min < z_xy < z_max; else output z_med. This removes impulses without flattening detail.
A larger window removes more noise but blurs more; a large median can delete thin lines. The adaptive window grows only where needed.

figure.caption: The nine window values and the same nine sorted: the 255 impulse falls to the last rank and the 5th value stays 11, so the median returns 11 while the mean (37.8) and midpoint (132) are dragged up by the impulse.

spec.title: One impulse in a 3×3 window
spec.aria: A 3×3 window holding one very bright 255 pixel, the same nine values in sorted order with the middle value 11 picked out, and the three results: mean 37.8, median 11, midpoint 132.

examples.question: A 3×3 window is 10, 12, 11 / 9, 255, 10 / 11, 10, 12. The true value is about 11 and 255 is an impulse. Find the arithmetic mean, median and midpoint, correct to one decimal place where needed.
steps: Sort the values: 9, 10, 10, 10, 11, 11, 12, 12, 255. The median is the 5th value = 11.
examples.answer: The arithmetic mean is 37.8, the median is 11 (correct), and the midpoint is 132; the median wins for impulse noise.
examples.check:
g = [10, 12, 11, 9, 255, 10, 11, 10, 12]
print(round(sum(g) / 9, 1))
s = sorted(g)
print(s[len(s) // 2])
print(int((min(g) + max(g)) / 2))

code.code:
g = [10, 12, 11, 9, 255, 10, 11, 10, 12]
total = sum(g)
mean = total / 9
s = sorted(g)
median = s[4]
midpoint = (min(g) + max(g)) / 2
print(round(mean, 1))
print(median)
print(int(midpoint))

traps: Using a mean filter on salt-and-pepper noise smears the impulse over the whole window instead of deleting it.
In the adaptive local filter, σ²ₙ/σ²_L goes to 1 in flat regions and to 0 at edges — not the other way round.
The max filter removes pepper (dark) noise; the min filter removes salt (bright) noise. Reversing them is a common exam slip.
For the contraharmonic filter, Q > 0 removes pepper and Q < 0 removes salt; check the sign before choosing Q.

quiz.q: What does the contraharmonic filter reduce to when Q = 0?
quiz.a: The arithmetic mean, because Σ g^{1} / Σ g^{0} = Σ g / MN.

quiz.q: Why is the median filter robust to salt-and-pepper impulses?
quiz.a: An impulse lands at an extreme rank after sorting, so the middle value is unchanged.

quiz.q: A 3×3 window has eight values equal to 10 and one centre value 250. Find the arithmetic mean (1 decimal place) and the median.
quiz.a: Sum = 8×10 + 250 = 330; mean = 330/9 = 36.7. Sorted values have median = 10.

quiz.q: In the adaptive local noise reduction filter, what happens to the weight σ²ₙ/σ²_L in a flat region and at an edge?
quiz.a: Flat region: σ²_L ≈ σ²ₙ, weight ≈ 1, output ≈ local mean. Edge: σ²_L ≫ σ²ₙ, weight ≈ 0, output ≈ observed pixel.

quiz.q: Which order-statistic filter removes salt (bright) noise: max or min?
quiz.a: Min, because it outputs the smallest value and ignores bright spikes.

quiz.q: In the adaptive median filter, what does the algorithm do if z_med is not between z_min and z_max?
quiz.a: It enlarges the window up to S_max; if the window reaches S_max, it outputs z_med.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern denoisers replace these fixed windows with bilateral filtering, non-local means and learned convolutional networks, but the adaptive median remains a fast first pass in camera pipelines. Search 'non-local means', 'BM3D', 'blind noise estimation' and 'adaptive median filter FPGA' to go further.
